title: Semantically Orthogonal Framework for Citation Classification: Disentangling Intent and Content

To evaluate label quality and framework clarity, we compute agreement between human annotators and LLMs. These experiments allow us to assess the reliability of our framework and explore the potential role of LLMs in future annotation workflows. To address the growing need for semantically robust, interpretable, and transferable citation annotations, we propose a new framework grounded in discourse intent and cited content structure. Before introducing its design, we first examine the limitations of existing classification frameworks that motivate our departure from conventional approaches. These limitations arise from structural entanglement, under-specified functional roles, and ambiguous referential targets, all of which hinder consistent annotation and downstream model performance. Despite the progress enabled by widely used frameworks such as CiTO [ 52 ] , ACL-ARC [ 28 ] , SciCite [ 14 ] , and ACT/ACT2 [ 45 , 40 ] , several structural limitations persist. These challenges reduce annotation clarity and consistency, hinder model generalization, and complicate the semantic interpretation of citation acts. We identify three interrelated problems: Many previous citation classification frameworks failed to separate the cited content type, such as method, data, or finding, from citation intent or function, such as use, and instead combined both dimensions into a single label.
